newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU centrists set realistic goal for Amsterdam.
newsitem.headline: EU centrists set realistic goal for Amsterdam.

text.p: European Union centrist leaders appeared on Wednesday to opt for realism over idealism ahead of two EU summit meetings designed to overhaul the Maastricht Treaty and ready the bloc for enlargement.

At a Brussels meeting of the European People's Party (EPP), a grouping of mainly Christian Democrat politicians, leaders signalled that the key task at next month's Amsterdam EU summit was to prepare for future enlargement.
Once that had been achieved, the EU could go on to settle important internal issues such as deeper integration, security and employment.
"We want (Amsterdam) to succeed at all costs. What is foremost in our minds is enlarging the Union," Wilfried Martens, former Belgian premier and current EPP chief, told reporters.

EPP leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and the Luxembourg, Belgian and Irish premiers, routinely meet to coordinate policy ahead of major EU summits.
EU heads of state and government are due to gather for an informal half-day session in the Dutch coastal resort of Noordwijk on Friday to continue preparations for the Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.

The Amsterdam summit is due to complete the 15-month inter-governmental conference (IGC), effectively a review of the bloc's "constitution", aimed at readying the Union to embrace up to a dozen ex-communist states from central and eastern Europe.

"We want a strong Europe. We want enlargement -- the fundamental objective -- to take place in a Europe with precise rules. That implies a reinforcement of the (Maastricht) treaty," Prodi told reporters.

Ireland's John Bruton, who faces an election just before the June summit, told Reuters there had been broad support for Kohl's realistic approach of going for what could be achieved at this stage and using that as a stepping-stone to further progress, on issues like deeper integration, later.
The message, according to the Irish premier was: "Don't overload the wagon but get enough on the wagon to reach the next stage."

As they left the four-hour "summit", during which they discussed a common position document for the two EU meetings, leaders said they hoped Friday's Noordwijk meeting would help pinpoint what had to be agreed in the Dutch capital next month.
"It is good that heads of government and state will take hold of the IGC issues, which up to now have fallen to foreign ministers," said Luxembourg premier Jean-Claude Juncker.
"Leaders will go home from Noordwijk knowing what they'll have to do at Amsterdam. Lots of things still have to be sorted out."
EU foreign ministers, meeting in The Hague on Tuesday, had appeared more optimistic on agreeing treaty reforms at Amsterdam after narrowing their differences on several key issues.
But European Parliament president Jose Maria Gil-Robles, attending the EPP meeting, suggested that an Amsterdam Treaty was by no means guaranteed.
"Let's hope that the Holy Spirit will shine on Amsterdam, so far we have not seen the light," he told reporters.
